title: One Model, Two Roles: Emergent Specialization in a Shared Recurrent Transformer
claim: One shared network reused with and without an input signal develops distinct specialized roles, shown through attention locality and commitment.
layout: 2 stacked rows, left-to-right, shared central block spanning both rows
description: Two dashed-border rows (L-update on top, H-update on bottom) flow left to right through one tall purple box labeled 'Shared Transformer' that spans both rows. In the top row, blue z_L, red z_H and green x-tilde boxes are summed and fed into the transformer. The output is z_L' (blue), followed by a blue grid showing local attention around a highlighted query cell, then a partially filled blue and grey grid labeled 'partial commit.' The bottom row mirrors this. Red z_H, blue z_L and a dashed red 'no x-tilde' box go in. The output is z_H' (red), then a fully red grid showing global attention, then a fully red grid labeled 'full commit.' Between the rows, italic text with arrows reads 'input asymmetry → functional specialization'. Color coding (blue for L, red for H) guides the eye.
caption: AIR testbed. The same shared Transformer $f(\cdot;\param)$ is reused at two positions in the recurrent schedule: with the encoded input $\xemb$ for L-updates (top) and without it for H-updates (bottom). Despite identical parameters, this input difference lets the shared model tell the two update types apart: $z_L$ behaves like a partially committed, revision-oriented state while $z_H$ behaves like a committed proposal state, and each query token in L-updates attends to other tokens more locally than H-updates.
abstract: Can a shared-weight recurrent Transformer---one that repeatedly applies the same Transformer to update evolving latent states---develop distinct internal roles without being partitioned into separate modules? We study this in Asymmetric Input Recurrence (AIR), a minimal two-state reasoning architecture in which the same Transformer model is reused for both updates (per literature, L and H) and the only built-in difference in the update rule is that the encoded input is injected during L-updates but not H-updates. Across Sudoku-Extreme and Maze, decoded rollouts reveal a consistent split: $z_H$ behaves like a fully committed proposal state, whereas $z_L$ retains local uncertainty and shifting intermediate structure. Freeze interventions provide evidence of dynamical dependence between the two states, with responses that vary across tasks, intervention directions, and seeds. Ablations show that to induce specialization, the shared model needs to be able to tell the two update types apart, either from input injection asymmetry or from a separate level token. Mechanistically, attention analysis shows that L-updates are consistently more local than H-updates in both Sudoku and Maze. Together, these results show that, in a two-state recurrent setting, a clear state-identity signal can induce stable, related functional roles inside a shared-parameter recurrent Transformer. Code is available at https://github.com/juchengshen/air.
